subject: Clarify when prefix-cache hits incur charges and contract implications
messages:
From: Jordan Hayes <jordan@olivethera.com>
To: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Olive Therapeutics Procurement <procurement@olivethera.com>
Date: Fri, 29 Jun 2028 15:20:00 -0400
Subject: Prefix cache billing — need clarification for our SOW

Hi Ben,

Thanks again for the demo last week — the latency gains were impressive. Before we move an SOW to procurement, we need a precise explanation of how Redwood bills when the hosted API returns a cached response. Two specific situations:

1) Multi-turn chat where a previously generated assistant response is returned from a prefix cache (exact match) — are any model compute tokens billed?
2) Partial hits where the prefix is matched but the model must continue generation (i.e., cached prefix + suffix generation) — how are input/output tokens attributed?

We have a high-volume automation workflow and want to understand when cache hits reduce our bill versus still triggering compute charges (and whether those count as "billed tokens" for commit thresholds). I attached a small sample of our prompts for context. Can you also point us to the exact wording in the rate card or contract addendum we should expect?

Appreciate a short breakdown and example math if possible.

—Jordan
Olive Therapeutics

From: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Hayes <jordan@olivethera.com>
Cc: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Fri, 29 Jun 2028 17:03:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Prefix cache billing — need clarification for our SOW

Jordan —

Short answer up front: if a request is served as a full, exact prefix-cache hit (we return the cached output without invoking the model runtime), Redwood does NOT bill model compute for that request. For mixed/partial scenarios where the cache supplies a prefix and the model must generate the remaining suffix, we bill for the tokens produced by the model runtime (the suffix tokens) plus any input tokens consumed if the runtime is invoked.

Quick examples (high level):
- Exact-response cache hit: 0 billed model tokens. (We still include the request in usage logs, and it counts toward usage analytics but not compute billing.)
- Partial hit + continuation: If the cache supplies first 40 tokens and the model generates 160 tokens to finish the reply, you are billed for the 160 generated tokens (and any minimal input token accounting tied to that invocation).
- Reranking / post-processing: If your request triggers additional server-side reranking or tool-calls that run the model, those will be billed as normal regardless of whether the initial prefix matched.

Edge cases we should watch out for: prefetching (warming the cache by proactively executing the model) is a compute action and will be billed; lingering session-affinity calls that touch the KV cache but also read context at runtime may be billed. Rishi — I've asked him to add the more technical detail below about soft vs hard hits and how we attribute them in metering.

I'll follow up with a short addendum you can include in your SOW and a redlined clause for the rate card.

Ben
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

From: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Hayes <jordan@olivethera.com>, Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>
Cc: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Sat, 30 Jun 2028 09:12:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Prefix cache billing — need clarification for our SOW

Jordan — adding the technical nuance so your engineering and procurement teams can parse the behaviors:

Definitions we use internally:
- Hard (exact) hit: the service can return the stored output payload without touching the model runtime. Metering marks these as cache-served and they do NOT generate compute token charges.
- Soft (partial) hit: a prefix (or prefix KV entries) matches, but the request requires the model to continue generation or to evaluate alternatives; the runtime is invoked and we bill for the portion of tokens produced by that invocation.

Metering rules (practical):
- If runtime invoked: we start counting billed tokens from the earliest token the model produces during that invocation. We do not double-bill for tokens that were provided by the cache.
- Input token attribution: for requests where we invoke the model, we account for the prompt tokens sent to the runtime. That means a partial-hit request will have input tokens + generated tokens billed, but the cached portion of the prompt (which was served without model execution) is not charged as runtime input.
- Prefetch/warm-up: any warming activity that executes the model (e.g., proactive prefill of KV entries by running the model on a sample prompt) generates normal compute charges. We can scope prefetches under a managed warming program to exclude them from billing, but that requires an explicit contract clause.

Operational notes:
- We label each request in the logs with a hit-type tag (HARD_HIT, SOFT_HIT, MISS) so your SRE can reconcile invoices to observed traffic.
- For streaming cases: if we stream a cached buffer and then open a live runtime stream for continuation, the streamed cached bytes are not billed; only the subsequent generated tokens are billed.

If you want I can generate a few concrete math examples using your sample prompts you attached — I included an annotated CSV in the attachments that maps examples to how they'd be metered.

—Rishi
Principal Architect, Serving Runtime

From: Mina Haddad <mina.haddad@redwood.com>
To: Jordan Hayes <jordan@olivethera.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben.carter@redwood.com>, Lauren Bishop <lauren.bishop@redwood.com>
Date: Mon, 02 Jul 2028 10:02:00 -0400
Subject: Re: Prefix cache billing — need clarification for our SOW

Jordan —

Thanks for raising this — from the commercial side we want to make sure Olive has predictability if you commit. A few practical offers based on what Ben and Rishi explained:

1) For the first 90 days after go-live we can apply a cache-hit protection credit: any request labeled HARD_HIT in our logs will be excluded from billed compute for the purpose of your initial commit attainment (i.e., they won't reduce your committed token balance). This helps you ramp without being penalized for legitimate warm-cache traffic.

2) For partial (SOFT_HIT) cases, those will count toward billing as Rishi described. However, we can apply a 10% rebate on billed tokens that are attributed to suffix generation for the first quarter as a concession tied to DL-2389.

3) We'll include explicit language in the SOW and rate card addendum clarifying: definitions of HARD_HIT/SOFT_HIT, prefetch behavior, and the reconciliation process (CSV logs + hit-type tags). I'll attach the proposed ratecard_v2.pdf and a sample amendment. If those look OK, we'll send a DocuSign amendment to Procurement (I linked the DocuSign below).

Attachments: ratecard_v2.pdf (rate card with proposed rebates), prefix_cache_examples.xlsx (metering examples), olive_prompt_samples.csv (your sample prompts annotated).

If Procurement wants this baked into a committed-usage discount tier, Lauren can scope the legal language and finalize the contract.

—Mina Haddad
Head of Revenue Operations, Redwood Inference
